name: Apache Thrift
summary: Facebook’s 2007 RPC framework: define types and services in one IDL file, generate clients and servers for over 20 languages, and pick the wire protocol and transport separately.
intro: You write structs, exceptions and services in a `.thrift` file, and the `thrift` compiler generates code for each language you need: data classes, a client stub and a processor that dispatches calls to your handler. Every field carries a number, and that number, not the name, goes on the wire. A reader that meets a field number it doesn’t know uses the type tag to skip it, so old and new versions of a service can talk during a staged rollout. A method takes arguments and returns one result or throws a declared exception; `oneway` methods send and don’t wait. There are no streaming methods in the IDL.

The runtime is a stack of swappable layers. A transport moves bytes (a socket, HTTP, a file, a memory buffer), optionally wrapped in a framed transport that prefixes each message with its length, which non-blocking servers need. A protocol turns values into bytes: binary writes big-endian integers and length-prefixed strings; compact uses variable-length zigzag integers and packs a small field-number delta and the type into one byte; JSON is human-readable. A server ties a transport, a protocol and the generated processor together, with thread-pool and non-blocking variants among others. Client and server must be configured with the same protocol and transport.

Thrift is an Apache top-level project, free under Apache 2.0, and still versioned 0.x after almost two decades (0.25.0 in September 2026). It sits inside much of the Hadoop world: the Hive Metastore and HiveServer2 speak Thrift, Impala uses it for client and internal calls, HBase runs a Thrift gateway for non-Java clients, and Parquet encodes its file metadata with Thrift. Meta keeps its own diverged fork, fbthrift.
strengths: One IDL generates code for more than 20 languages, from C++, Java, Go and Python to Erlang, OCaml, Delphi and Smalltalk
Protocol and transport are chosen independently: compact binary over a socket for speed, JSON over HTTP for debugging or browsers
Numbered fields with skip-unknown semantics make adding or removing fields safe across versions
Mature and embedded in widely used systems (Hive, Impala, HBase, Parquet), so it is well tested in production
limits: No streaming methods, and no deadline that travels with each call as gRPC’s does
Language libraries differ in features and minimum versions, tracked in a matrix the project itself says may not be correct in all cases; it has never reached 1.0
Client and server must be set up with the same protocol and transport (binary, compact or JSON; framed or not): HBase’s guide, for one, notes that a framed server needs a matching client setting

story: As Facebook grew, its search, ad selection and event logging had outgrown its LAMP stack. Engineers wrote back-end services in whatever language fit best, mostly C++, Java and Python, while the website was PHP, so they needed a fast, reliable way to call across languages. The authors found that existing options were too limited, too inflexible about data types, or too slow; their paper dismissed SOAP for its XML parsing overhead and CORBA as heavyweight, and noted that Google’s Protocol Buffers were closed-source. Thrift succeeded Pillar, a similar system Adam D’Angelo had started at Caltech and continued at Facebook.

Mark Slee, Aditya Agarwal and Marc Kwiatkowski described Thrift in an April 2007 paper, and Facebook open-sourced it that month with five target languages: C++, Java, Python, Ruby and PHP. It already carried Facebook’s search service and structured logging. Thrift entered the Apache Incubator in May 2008 and became a top-level Apache project in October 2010.

Hadoop-era projects adopted it widely: Cassandra’s older client API, HBase’s gateway, Hive’s servers and Parquet’s metadata all used Thrift. In 2015 Google open-sourced gRPC, built on Protocol Buffers and HTTP/2, which now covers much of the same ground, and Cassandra removed its Thrift interface in 4.0. Thrift lives on inside the systems that built on it.

choices.choice: Static code generation instead of a dynamic system
choices.why: Generating code ahead of time produces validated code that runs without run-time type introspection, and the developer describes a whole service in one short file.

The paper argued that whether a service uses XML or binary is immaterial to the application, and the same data should flow over sockets, memory or files. Splitting the layers let Facebook add framing, buffering or a new encoding without touching generated code.

Facebook needed staged rollouts and old log files to keep working. A field identifier plus a type tag lets a reader skip anything it doesn’t recognise, and argument lists are structs too, so method signatures can evolve safely.

The first binary protocol deliberately skipped tricks like 7-bit variable-length integers to keep the code clear. The compact protocol, with varints and field-number deltas, was added later when size mattered.
